1.pericope_label: Zacchaeus, chief among the publicans, ran before and climbed up into a sycomore tree

schools.summary: Ellicott reconstructs the Roman farming system that left Zacchaeus a middle-man between the capitalists of the equestrian order and the actual collectors, with as many chances of enriching himself as a Turkish pacha, and settles the sycomore as the fig-mulberry, Luke’s care to distinguish it from the sycamine being the accuracy one expects of a physician; Robertson notes the word for chief publican occurs nowhere else; Barnes finds the wealth recorded because it was so unlikely a rich man should follow one so despised, and reads the seeking as plain curiosity; Lightfoot rejects the identification with the Zaccai who fathered Rabban Jochanan.
Gill observes that Christ passed straight through Jericho, having no work there.

Clarke turns the man’s shortness into an advantage, since had he been as tall as the rest he might have passed unnoticed, and holds that even the imperfections of our persons may be made subservient to grace; Wesley calls the office a very honourable and profitable place and sees desire conquering honour and shame.

Henry notes that Jericho was built under a curse and yet honoured with Christ’s presence, that Christ did not study to show himself and was lost in a crowd on a day of humiliation, and that the man forgot the gravity of his office and ran ahead like a boy.

Titus Bostrensis takes the seeking for a seed of salvation already sprung, since none who truly sees Jesus can remain in wickedness, and names two obstacles, the crowd and the man’s smallness, the multitude that hindered him being not so much of men as of his sins.

Ambrose asks why this man’s stature alone is described and suggests he was young in wickedness or weak in faith, since one who could climb was not yet prostrate in sin; Bede reads the Latin name for the tree, the foolish fig, and makes it the Cross, which sustains believers as the fig sustains its fruit and is mocked by unbelievers as foolishness.

positions.view: Simple curiosity, which God used as he uses every principle
Not mere curiosity, which would not have won the Lord’s warm approval
A seed of salvation already springing in him

outliers.claim: Reconstructs Jericho’s trade in Gilead balsam, dates and palm-honey to explain how a sub-contractor in the Roman revenue could grow rich, comparing his opportunities to those of a Turkish pacha.

themes: And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho.
And, behold, there was a man named Zaccheus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich.
And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature.
And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way.

5.pericope_label: Make haste and come down: this day is salvation come to this house

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that Jericho was then a city of the priests, so the Lord passed over their houses to lodge with a publican, and that the murmur came from the whole crowd rather than a party of Pharisees; Robertson hears the compound verb as onomatopoetic, like the cooing of doves or the hum of bees, and renders the command come down in a hurry; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic cap on almsgiving at a fifth, decreed at Usha, which Zacchaeus far exceeds; Barnes calls it one among a thousand instances where the Saviour goes beyond the desert and expectation of men.

Calvin makes it a remarkable favour that the Lord anticipates the man and asks lodging of his own accord, though it was a greater gift to dwell in his heart than to enter his house, and turns the murmuring back on the murmurers, since the world disregards the offer of grace and complains when it is carried to others.
Wesley alone softens the murmur, holding that most spoke from surprise rather than indignation.
Henry hears in the restitution a present deed and not a bequest, and guesses the man had heard how the rich young ruler broke with Christ over such a command.

Theophylact reckons that nothing was left of the man’s own estate, and marks the tense — not I will give, but I give; Pseudo-Chrysostom presses that he does not wait for the judgment of the law but makes himself his own judge, and answers the objection from Paul’s rule about eating with the covetous by observing that these were converts, not persistent offenders.
Cyril of Alexandria says of the calling that Christ calls near those afar off and gives light to those in darkness.

Ambrose says he invites himself uninvited, seeing the will before he heard the word; Bede grounds the title son of Abraham in imitation rather than descent, and finds in the word also a declaration that those raised out of injustice belong to the sons of promise.

debates.question: What does sinner mean when the crowd applies it to Zacchaeus?

positions.view: Not what we ordinarily call a sinner — collecting taxes was no crime in itself
The popular Pharisaic sense, attaching necessarily to his calling

outliers.claim: Infers from the fourfold restitution that the estate cannot have been wholly unjust gains, since otherwise nothing would have remained out of which to restore fourfold after giving half away.

themes: And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zaccheus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house.
And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully.
And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner.
And Zaccheus stood, and said unto the Lord; Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.
And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham.
For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.

11.pericope_label: A certain nobleman went into a far country: occupy till I come

schools.summary: Barnes explains that a prince under Rome had to go to the capital for recognition, as Archelaus and Antipas did before Augustus, which made the parable perfectly intelligible to its hearers; Robertson adds that this had happened while Jesus was a boy in Nazareth and was common knowledge, and renders the command while I am coming rather than till I come; Ellicott draws the consequence of starting from equality where Matthew starts from unequal ability, that the trust here is what all disciples hold in common; Barnes also denies the number ten denotes anything in particular.

Calvin says the disciples were aiming at the shadow of a kingdom, and refuses all subtleties about the far country, which expresses nothing but a long absence from his death to his last coming, since he reigns now in regenerating his people though that way of reigning is hidden from the flesh; Gill takes ten for a round number, the apostles being twelve, and the servants for ministers rather than the elect, since one proved wicked.

Clarke distinguishes two morals in the parable — the citizens’ rejection and its punishment in the destruction of their state, which alone answers the words about the kingdom appearing immediately, and the servants’ reward, which is all Matthew’s talents intend — and calls ten a sacred number among the Hebrews.

Chrysostom compares Luke’s pounds with Matthew’s talents, noting that here different sums come out of the same principal while there each servant doubles his own, so the rewards differ too, and takes ten for a sign of perfection since one who counts beyond it begins again from unity; Eusebius and Theophylact read the journey as the ascension and the return as the second appearing.

Cyril observes that Christ calls himself first a man, then noble, but not yet a king, since at his first appearing he exercised no kingly power, and identifies the hostile citizens as those who told Pilate they had no king but Caesar.

Augustine reads the ten pounds as the law because of the commandments and the ten servants as those to whom grace was preached under it, and says the message sent after the nobleman continued past the resurrection in the persecution of the apostles; Bede gives one pound to each because there is one doctrine, one faith, one baptism.

debates.question: Does the number ten signify anything?

positions.view: Yes — a sign of perfection, or the ten commandments
No — a round number and a circumstance of the narrative

outliers.claim: Protests that rendering the mina as a pound is an impropriety any reader can see, and insists the original word should be retained.

themes: And as they heard these things, he added and spake a parable, because he was nigh to Jerusalem, and because they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear.
He said therefore, A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom, and to return.
And he called his ten servants, and delivered them ten pounds, and said unto them, Occupy till I come.
But his citizens hated him, and sent a message after him, saying, We will not have this man to reign over us.

And it came to pass, that when he was returned, having received the kingdom, then he commanded these servants to be called unto him, to whom he had given the money, that he might know how much every man had gained by trading.

16.pericope_label: Thou hast been faithful in a very little: unto every one which hath shall be given

schools.summary: Ellicott observes that these servants gain tenfold where Matthew’s merely double, and compares the thirty, sixty and hundredfold of the sower; he also presses that authority over ten cities must answer to some real work of guidance in the unseen world and cannot be reduced to the beatific vision, and identifies the napkin as a cloth used then as now for hoarding money. Robertson traces austere to a verb meaning to dry up, rough to the taste and then harsh in disposition, thinks the phrase about taking up what one laid not down a proverb for a grasping profiteer, insists the increase demanded is legal interest and not usury, and suspects the bystanders really interrupted. Barnes warns the cities are not to be looked for literally and states plainly that men keep their talents unused.

Clarke distinguishes the mina, given alike to all who hear the gospel, from the talents, which answer to differing capacities, and reports that the bystanders’ verse is missing from Codex Bezae and some copies of the Itala; Wesley agrees interest is contrary to no law of God or man but denies it is any plea for oppression, and hears admiration rather than envy in the objection.

Chrysostom draws the governing contrast, that in earthly wealth none is made rich without another being made poor, but in spiritual riches none is enriched without enriching another; Theophylact notes that a napkin covers the face of the dead, so the idler left his pound dead and unprofitable, and says the enemies were slain even in this world by the Roman army.

Bede makes the first servant the teachers sent to the circumcision and the second those sent to the uncircumcision, whose pound gained five by converting nations enslaved to the five senses, and makes the money the preaching of the gospel to be put into hearts ready for it; Ambrose takes the ten cities for souls, since as Jerusalem is called a city so are peace-making souls; Augustine takes the bank for the public profession of religion, applies the napkin to those who say each need answer only for himself, and turns the sentence on the enemies against the Marcionists.

debates.question: What is the bank the servant should have used?

positions.view: Hearts ready to receive the preached word
The public profession of religion itself
Simply a money-changer’s table, the interest being lawful and not usurious

outliers.claim: Uses the command to slay the enemies against the Marcionists, who allow Christ to be good while calling the God of the Old Testament evil, since here the Son does what they impute to the Father alone.

themes: Then came the first, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds.
And he said unto him, Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities.
And the second came, saying, Lord, thy pound hath gained five pounds.
And he said likewise to him, Be thou also over five cities.
And another came, saying, Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin:
For I feared thee, because thou art an austere man: thou takest up that thou layedst not down, and reapest that thou didst not sow.
And he saith unto him, Out of thine own mouth will I judge thee, thou wicked servant. Thou knewest that I was an austere man, taking up that I laid not down, and reaping that I did not sow:
Wherefore then gavest not thou my money into the bank, that at my coming I might have required mine own with usury?
And he said unto them that stood by, Take from him the pound, and give it to him that hath ten pounds.
(And they said unto him, Lord, he hath ten pounds.)
For I say unto you, That unto every one which hath shall be given; and from him that hath not, even that he hath shall be taken away from him.
But those mine enemies, which would not that I should reign over them, bring hither, and slay them before me.

28.pericope_label: The Lord hath need of him: if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the Greek word for descent occurs in no other New Testament writer, a technical geographical term natural to one who may have studied Strabo, finds it characteristic of the Gentile Evangelist that glory replaces the Hosanna of the others, and takes the objecting Pharisees for the party that had granted Christ respect as a Teacher; Robertson places the procession on the southern slope where the city bursts suddenly into view and hears enthusiasm pent up since the parable, and reads the objectors as half-hearted followers inside the procession; Barnes takes the answer about the stones as proverbial.
Wesley thinks the multitude spoke from a divine impulse words most of them did not understand.

Henry finds Christ foremost of the company, going forward bound in the spirit and knowing what awaited him, observes drily that many will attend Christ at other people’s expense who care to be at no charge upon him themselves, sets the disciples’ song beside the angels’ so that each rejoices in what the other gains, and claims a literal fulfilment of the stones crying out when the earth quaked and the rocks rent.

Titus Bostrensis says those who saw him going up thought he meant to begin the kingdom there, and only after the parable had corrected the error did he go forward to his passion; Chrysostom marks a change of manner, since having proved his power he now transacts everything with the highest authority, foretelling the unbroken colt and that none would hinder them.

Origen reads Bethany as the house of obedience and Bethphage as the house of cheek-bones, a priestly name because those parts of a sacrifice fell to the priests, and says the colt had many masters until the Saviour had need of him and then had no other, since none can serve God and mammon.

Bede places Bethphage on Mount Olivet as a village of the priests; Ambrose finds the colt unable to be loosed except at the Lord’s command, takes it for the Gentile people on whom no man had sat, sets the two masteries against each other — others bind to possess, Christ looses to keep — and gives the sitting an inward sense, the mystical Ruler taking his seat in the depths of men’s souls, his word at once a rein and a goad; Augustine settles the discrepancy between the Gospels, since where both an ass and a colt may be conceived there is no variance; the Gloss notes the disciples served him with their own clothes as well as another man’s colt.

debates.question: Are the crying stones a proverb or a prediction?

positions.view: Proverbial, meaning only that such joy could not properly be restrained
Literally fulfilled at the crucifixion, when the earth quaked and the rocks rent

outliers.claim: Contrasts the two kinds of mastery over the tied colt: others bind in order to possess, while Christ looses in order to keep, knowing that gifts are stronger than chains.

themes: And when he had thus spoken, he went before, ascending up to Jerusalem.
And it came to pass, when he was come nigh to Bethphage and Bethany, at the mount called the mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples,
Saying, Go ye into the village over against you; in the which at your entering ye shall find a colt tied, whereon yet never man sat: loose him, and bring him hither.
And if any man ask you, Why do ye loose him? thus shall ye say unto him, Because the Lord hath need of him.
And they that were sent went their way, and found even as he had said unto them.
And as they were loosing the colt, the owners thereof said unto them, Why loose ye the colt?
And they said, The Lord hath need of him.
And they brought him to Jesus: and they cast their garments upon the colt, and they set Jesus thereon.
And as he went, they spread their clothes in the way.

And when he was come nigh, even now at the descent of the mount of Olives, the whole multitude of the disciples began to rejoice and praise God with a loud voice for all the mighty works that they had seen;
Saying, Blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord: peace in heaven, and glory in the highest.
And some of the Pharisees from among the multitude said unto him, Master, rebuke thy disciples.
And he answered and said unto them, I tell you that, if these should hold their peace, the stones would immediately cry out.

41.pericope_label: He beheld the city, and wept over it: thou knewest not the time of thy visitation

schools.summary: Ellicott finds in the repeated pronoun the strongest possible emotion and in the unfinished clause the deepest human sorrow the Son of Man had known, notes that the tense with now implies a concealment already completed, and explains that the word for the siege-work means first a stake, then the stockade of a besieger’s camp, then the earthwork it stood on — the embankment rather than the excavation, one of a cluster of terms peculiar to Luke and belonging to the higher forms of historical composition; Robertson names the figure aposiopesis; Lightfoot sets the rabbinic explanations of the ruin beside Christ’s.

Calvin says the discourse is pathetic and therefore abrupt, since men under vehement passion never more than half express their feelings, hears a lament and a reproach mingled, takes even thou for a silent contrast with every other city, and draws the rule that men deserve heavier punishment in proportion to the gifts received.
Wesley says simply that Titus performed the siege exactly.

Henry notes that we never read Christ laughed but often find him in tears, that David had wept in this very place with his men of war, and that he wept in the midst of his triumph while all about him rejoiced; he states plainly that there is a time of visitation in which the things belonging to our peace may be known to good purpose, and that none are so blind as those who will not see.

Eusebius says his coming was to bring peace to those near and afar off, and that because they would not receive it, it was hidden from them; Theophylact glosses the visitation as Christ’s own coming, and says that had they believed they might have been reconciled to the Romans as those who believed were.

Origen observes that Christ confirms his own beatitudes by example, having said blessed are they that weep and then wept over the city; Cyril takes the tears for the token of a real humanity, and asks whether the weeping may not also concern the spiritual Jerusalem, since no Gentile is wept over but only one who was of Jerusalem and has ceased to be.

Gregory says the Redeemer does not cease to weep through his elect whenever he sees any turn from a good life, describes the corrupt soul as having its day because it shuns any foresight of the future, identifies the overthrow as that of Vespasian and Titus attested by Josephus, and turns the visitation inward, since a soul that knows not its time is given over at the last to its enemies.

positions.view: The city that fell for the wickedness of its inhabitants
Also the spiritual Jerusalem, since one who sins after receiving the mysteries of truth is wept over

outliers.claim: Sets against Christ’s reason for the ruin the rabbinic ones — that Jerusalem was destroyed for nothing but profanation of the sabbath, or for nothing but neglect of the phylacteries.

themes: And when he was come near, he beheld the city, and wept over it,
Saying, If thou hadst known, even thou, at least in this thy day, the things which belong unto thy peace! but now they are hid from thine eyes.
For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,
And shall lay thee even with the ground, and thy children within thee; and they shall not leave in thee one stone upon another; because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.

45.pericope_label: My house is the house of prayer: the people were very attentive to hear him

schools.summary: Robertson notes that the first men of the people stand after the verb and apart from the chief priests and scribes, which marks them as a distinct group, and that it was the raising of Lazarus that brought the leaders of Jerusalem together for his destruction; Ellicott identifies them as notables of the city, whether members of the Sanhedrin or not.

Calvin draws from the plot a description of the Church, which consisted of the despised multitude while its enemies were the guardians of religion — part of the folly of the cross, that God passes by the excellence of the world and chooses what is foolish and weak — and adds that even with good ground for pursuing Christ they had no right to proceed to murder after the manner of robbers, the conspiracy being frustrated because by God’s secret purpose he was appointed to the death of the cross.
Theophylact recalls that Christ had cleansed the temple at the outset of his preaching and did it again because the crime had grown by their not being chastened.

Origen puts the sharpest form of the charge, that if he sells what the Holy Spirit revealed to him, or will not teach without a fee, he is selling a dove; Cyril explains that animals were sold for the sacrifices by the custom of the law, but that the shadows were passing and the truth of Christ shining, so the customs were reformed and the house left a house of prayer.

Gregory notes that having foretold the city’s ruin he went straight in to eject the traders, which shows the destruction arose chiefly from the guilt of the priests, and defines the two trades — the sellers part at a price with what is another’s by right, since to sell justice is to keep it only for a reward, while the buyers, unwilling to do what is just, purchase sin by paying their patrons; Ambrose says God will not have his temple a house of traffic, nor the priestly service a saleable performance of religion, and drives out the money-changers as those who seek gain from the divine Scripture; Augustine takes the temple for Christ in his human nature and then for the Church joined to him, signifying men who shelter there to conceal their wickedness; Bede offers three grounds for the resolve to kill him and two readings of their inability to act.

debates.question: Why could the rulers not act against him?

positions.view: They feared a tumult of the people
They sought his death precisely because their authority was set aside and the crowds flocked to hear him

outliers.claim: Turns the sale of doves on the preacher himself: if he sells for money what the Holy Spirit has revealed to him, or refuses to teach without hire, he is selling the Holy Spirit.

themes: And he went into the temple, and began to cast out them that sold therein, and them that bought;
Saying unto them, It is written, My house is the house of prayer: but ye have made it a den of thieves.
And he taught daily in the temple. But the chief priests and the scribes and the chief of the people sought to destroy him,
And could not find what they might do: for all the people were very attentive to hear him.
